title: Working-Memory Load Laboratory
scopeNote: This keeps the performed load task and the factorial that makes the point: load crossed with the domain of the concurrent task. Neither factor can go, because one line falling with load shows only that load costs something. The third load level, the practice trials with feedback on every one, and the fuller treatment of what separable parts means stay in the longer version.
summary: Hold two letters or six in mind, do four paced judgements about something else, then pick the letters out of a grid. The cost of the extra load depends on whether the in-between task is made of the same material as the letters.
learningObjectives: Describe a concurrent-task design and say what the retention interval is for.
Explain why the domain of the concurrent task matters, not just its presence.
Read an interaction between load and concurrent-task domain from two lines.
Explain why a single pool of general effort predicts the two lines falling together.
Identify unmatched task difficulty and small cell sizes as limits on the conclusion.
interactionTypes: two practice trials with the answers shown
a performed block of 20 trials crossing two loads with two concurrent domains
a paced retention interval that moves on without the learner
recall by picking the held letters out of a grid that grows with the load
two lines whose separation is the finding
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Everything is scored in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with every response a labelled button. The display description names the letters to be held, states the in-between question in words, and at recall says how many letters to pick and how many are in the grid. Recall picks are marked with aria-pressed as well as a colour and a glyph, and can be undone by pressing again. Only the retention judgements are paced, which is stated in the setup note and is deliberate; nothing else is timed out. The chart distinguishes the two lines by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour and names them in a key with a sample of each, and carries a description giving all four points. Where too few trials are completed the chart and table are hidden rather than drawn empty.
dataStatus: The learner's own recall, produced in the moment. Nothing is a norm and nothing is compared with anyone else.
simulationNotes: Twenty trials crossing loads of 2 and 6 letters with a verbal or a spatial concurrent task, five per cell. The recall grid holds the targets plus an equal number of lures, so it grows with the load: a fixed grid would be a serious confound, because with eight options a load of 2 offers six lures and a load of 6 offers two, and guessing would score 25 per cent at the low load against 75 per cent at the high one. One lure per target holds chance at 50 per cent whatever the load. Recall is by picking from the grid rather than by a single yes-or-no probe, which would yield one bit per trial and far too little to draw anything from five trials. The retention judgements are paced and move on without an answer, which is stated on the page: a self-paced filler can be rushed or ignored while rehearsing, and then it is not a load at all. The two concurrent tasks are matched for pacing and number of judgements but not for difficulty, and the caution says so.
readmeTopic: why what you are doing in between matters as much as how much you are holding
